clue.text: Hospital cut that avoids issue

parts.note: a surgical operation whose whole purpose is to stop a man fathering children; issue here means offspring, not a problem

explanation.surface: A hospital trimming its budget in a way that sidesteps controversy.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'cut' as a spending cut and 'issue' as a contentious matter and the clue is about politics; really the cut is surgical and the issue is children.
explanation.definitionFit: The procedure severs the sperm ducts, so a man who has it fathers no offspring, which is what issue means in legal language.

clue.text: Trendily experienced in our ways?

parts.note: someone hip and shrewd, read whimsically as wise in the ways, that is the roads, around us

explanation.walkthrough: Ways are roads, so being wise in them is being wise in the street: the hyphenated word describes a person savvy about urban life.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective describes someone with the shrewdness and know-how gained from modern city living.

clue.text: Knocking off, swallowing Ecstasy (large) Blair would distance himself from it

definitions.text: Blair would distance himself from it

indicators.note: the word for stealing takes the two single letters into itself, as a mouth swallows food

parts.note: knocking off is slang for stealing, a theft
L is the clothing-size abbreviation for large
E is the drugs slang abbreviation for Ecstasy

explanation.surface: A tabloid story of a drug-fuelled burglary from which Tony Blair would keep his distance.
explanation.walkthrough: L and E go in after the first three letters of THEFT. Tony Blair rebranded his party as New Labour, steering it away from its traditional socialist wing.
explanation.definitionFit: Blair's New Labour project deliberately moved the party towards the centre, away from the socialist wing of politics.

clue.text: Dirty film Ceausescu made internally

indicators.note: the answer sits inside the run of letters across the two words, not at either edge

explanation.surface: The Romanian dictator Ceausescu producing a sordid movie at home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dirty film' looks like a smutty movie, but it is the layer of grime on a liquid's surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Scum is the layer of froth and dirt that forms on a liquid, a film of filth.

clue.text: Would-be big shot dictator?

parts.note: a dictator who hoped to be a big shot, and who in the 1990s news commissioned a giant gun to fire huge shells

explanation.walkthrough: The Iraqi leader was famous for his 'supergun' project, a cannon meant to fire enormous shells: a would-be big shot in two senses.
explanation.definitionFit: The Iraqi ruler held absolute power for decades and sought prestige weapons such as the giant Project Babylon cannon.

clue.text: It protects the likes of that which craps all over the place!

definitions.text: It protects the likes of that which craps all over the place!

indicators.note: scattered everywhere, so the five letters of the word before are jumbled

explanation.surface: A charity defending creatures that relieve themselves anywhere they like.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both definition and wordplay: the jumbled word gives the British animal-welfare charity, the Royal Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals, which protects pets and other beasts that foul everywhere.
explanation.definitionFit: The Royal Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals protects animals, which notoriously foul anywhere.

clue.text: Show that gets the lads to act the wolf and gawp?

parts.note: to bay is to howl like a wolf or hound
to gawp is to stare, to watch

explanation.surface: A TV show that makes young men leer and ogle like wolves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Act the wolf' suggests wolf-whistling at women; here it is howling. Baywatch was the 1990s TV series famous for lifeguards in swimsuits.
explanation.definitionFit: Baywatch was a long-running American television series about Californian lifeguards, so it is a programme.

clue.text: Crown pursues strife — and this delivers the killing blow

indicators.note: one piece follows behind the other, so the head word comes after the conflict word

parts.note: strife, conflict, means war
the crown is the top of the head

explanation.surface: Royal power chasing conflict, ending with a lethal strike.
explanation.definitionFit: The explosive tip of a missile is what detonates and does the destruction.

clue.text: Left, involved in principle worth fighting for, figure this is not for New Labour!

definitions.text: this is not for New Labour!

indicators.note: the letter for left becomes wrapped up inside the principle word

parts.note: a cause is a principle people campaign or fight for
four is a figure, a number

explanation.surface: A socialist principle of the left, once worth a fight, that New Labour has abandoned.
explanation.walkthrough: Clause Four of the Labour Party constitution committed it to common ownership; Tony Blair had it rewritten in 1995 as part of creating New Labour.
explanation.definitionFit: Blair's modernisers scrapped the old nationalisation pledge in the party constitution, so New Labour rejected it.

clue.text: The ultimate in transport?

parts.note: ultimate read as final: the last vehicle anyone rides in, to their funeral

explanation.walkthrough: 'The ultimate' sounds like a luxury limousine; it means the final journey.
explanation.definitionFit: The vehicle carrying a coffin to the funeral is literally the last conveyance a person takes.

clue.text: Vulnerable type, male, screwed with nothing on

indicators.note: in an across answer, having something on means it is attached after
twisted, wrenched out of shape, so the letters of male are rearranged

parts.note: a duck is a score of nothing in cricket

explanation.surface: A defenceless man who was had sex with while naked.
explanation.walkthrough: A duck is zero runs in cricket, a common crossword stand-in for nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: A lame duck is a weak or ineffectual person or organisation, easily picked off.

clue.text: Exposing organs, the Eye's scandalous way?

definitions.text: Exposing organs, the Eye's scandalous way?

parts.words: Exposing organs, the Eye's scandalous way
parts.note: organs are newspapers; Private Eye's mocking name for the road where Britain's press used to be based

explanation.walkthrough: 'Exposing organs' suggests indecent exposure; organs are the newspapers that expose scandals. Private Eye calls Fleet Street, the old home of the London press, by this name.
explanation.definitionFit: Private Eye's satirical nickname for Fleet Street, the London thoroughfare synonymous with the British newspaper industry.

clue.text: Constitution needs attention — Dorrell's responsibility, supposedly

parts.note: one's constitution is one's physical state, one's health
care means attention, as in take care

explanation.surface: A political constitution requiring attention, a job a minister is meant to handle.
explanation.walkthrough: Stephen Dorrell was the Conservative Health Secretary in the mid-1990s; 'supposedly' is a dig at how well he did it.
explanation.definitionFit: As Secretary of State for Health, Dorrell was in charge of the National Health Service and medical provision.

clue.text: Party — it's unhappy on the left!

parts.note: a social is a party, a gathering

indicators.note: the letters are upset, out of sorts, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: A political party that is miserable about being on the left.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Party' looks political but is a social gathering; the letters of IT'S become IST.
explanation.definitionFit: Socialist politics sit on the left of the political spectrum, so the adjective means left-wing.

clue.text: City needs nuts — clear?

parts.note: nuts means crazy, mad
to clear something away is to rid a place of it

explanation.surface: A town that has to be cleared of lunatics.
explanation.definitionFit: Madrid is the capital of Spain.

clue.text: Make as if on heroin, perhaps

indicators.note: signals that the letters may be arranged otherwise, so they are shuffled

parts.note: H is drugs slang for heroin

explanation.surface: Pretending to be high on drugs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Make as if' reads as pretend; 'Make' alone is the definition, and AS IF, ON and the heroin letter all go into the jumble.
explanation.definitionFit: To fashion something is to make or shape it, a verb of construction.

clue.text: See 5
No, Norman lost it in Europe's first and last hi-jack location

indicators.note: the letters before it are placed inside the pair of letters from Europe that follow

parts.note: the first and last letters of Europe are both E
N is the abbreviation for no, as on a yes/no form

indicators.note: the surname loses those two letters, which simply drop away

parts.note: Norman Tebbit, the Conservative politician
taken as written

explanation.surface: Norman Tebbit saying no and losing his temper over Europe, which he famously opposed.
explanation.walkthrough: Norman Tebbit was a Eurosceptic Conservative cabinet minister of the Thatcher years. Entebbe was the Ugandan airport of the 1976 hijacking and Israeli rescue raid.
explanation.definitionFit: Entebbe airport in Uganda is where hijacked Air France passengers were held in 1976 before an Israeli raid freed them.

clue.text: Court action — the old man's habit?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a lawsuit to establish who fathered a child
second meaning, whimsical: pater is Latin for father, the old man

explanation.walkthrough: 'The old man' is slang for father, and a suit is a set of clothes, a habit.
explanation.definitionFit: A legal claim seeking to prove a man fathered a child is the standard name for this kind of court case.

clue.text: Victoria wasn't terribly mad about manhandling

indicators.note: the jumbled letters go around the other piece
badly, so the letters of mad are put in a disordered arrangement

parts.note: manhandling is rough use of something

explanation.surface: Queen Victoria was most displeased by being pushed around.
explanation.walkthrough: Queen Victoria is said to have declared 'We are not amused', so the definition is the missing word of her famous remark.
explanation.definitionFit: The famous quotation attributed to the queen completes the phrase: she was not entertained.

clue.text: Issued a writ, reportedly — who does he think he's kidding?

definitions.text: who does he think he's kidding?

indicators.note: signals that the word is heard rather than read, as in a spoken report

parts.note: to issue a writ against someone is to sue them

explanation.surface: A writ was served, apparently, on a man who is fooling nobody.
explanation.walkthrough: The P is silent, so the answer is pronounced like 'sued'.
explanation.definitionFit: A pseud is a pretentious person whose intellectual airs are a bluff, someone fooling only himself.

clue.text: Les excited, about to breath heavily — creep!

indicators.note: the jumbled letters go around the other piece
stirred up, so the letters of Les are rearranged

parts.note: to huff is to breathe heavily, puffing

explanation.surface: An aroused man called Les panting heavily, a real creep.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Creep' looks like a noun for the panting Les, but it is a verb meaning to move slowly.
explanation.definitionFit: To shuffle is to walk slowly dragging the feet, much as to creep is to move slowly and quietly.

clue.text: See 9
Conservative function, protecting English language?

indicators.note: the function word surrounds and shields the English letter

parts.note: a role is a function

explanation.surface: A Tory duty to defend the English language.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Language' looks like part of the English phrase but stands alone as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A creole is a mother tongue formed from a mix of languages, such as Haitian Creole.

clue.text: Cartland lover grabs former city desk

indicators.note: the lover takes hold of the city, enclosing it

parts.note: a beau is a lover, the sort of hero in Barbara Cartland's romantic novels
Ur was an ancient Mesopotamian city

explanation.surface: A romantic hero from a Barbara Cartland novel seizes a desk.
explanation.walkthrough: Barbara Cartland was a prolific British writer of romance novels; Ur is the crossword's favourite ancient city.
explanation.definitionFit: A bureau is a writing desk with drawers and a sloping lid.

clue.text: Maybe Thatcher the boozer gets your second in

parts.note: a boozer is British slang for a pub, a bar
one's is the impersonal form of your

explanation.surface: Margaret Thatcher at the pub getting in the second round.
explanation.walkthrough: Margaret Thatcher was made a life peer in 1992; 'Maybe' marks her as one example.
explanation.definitionFit: After leaving the Commons, Thatcher received a peerage and the title of a female noble in the House of Lords.
